title: US designates Palestine Action a terrorist group
description: The US has imposed sanctions on Palestine Action, designating it as a terrorist group.The US Department of the Treasury said it had "taken action" aga
body: The US has imposed sanctions on Palestine Action, designating it as a terrorist group.The US Department of the Treasury said it had "taken action" against the UK-based group, which it accused of supporting "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020". Supporting Palestine Action became illegal in the UK in 2025 after the government banned it under anti-terror legislation.The group's co-founder Huda Ammori responded in a social media post, saying: "As a Palestinian and Iraqi, the fact the country which destroyed both my homelands is calling me a terrorist, is beyond hypocritical."In a statement to the BBC, Ammori said the group's actions had "always been about saving lives", adding the ban should be a "wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and democracy".Announcing the move in a statement on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Far-left extremists, their fronts, and their enablers should be on notice: We will bring the full weight of our economic tools to bear."Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated."The sanctions imposed include freezing any assets belonging to the group that are either based in the US or in the control of US citizens.The US ban on the group is part of a wave of sanctions announced by the Trump administration against what it says are far-left terror organisations around the world.The Department of Treasury accused Palestine Action of having supported "numerous acts of terrorism since July 2020, including acts that have physically injured UK law enforcement personnel, as well as acts intended to intimidate lawful commercial enterprises and coerce the UK government".Palestine Action, which used so-called direct action tactics against Israeli-linked arms companies in the UK, has been facing an ongoing legal battle to get its UK ban overturned. In June, Court of Appeal judges ruled the UK government made a "justified and proportionate" interference on freedom of expression rights. But Palestine Action has since been given permission to challenge the decision at the Supreme Court.More than 2,000 people are facing potential trial after being arrested for protesting against the ban by allegedly declaring their support for a proscribed terrorism group during mass demonstrations.Separately, four of its members were jailed in June for a break-in at a defence firm that caused more than £1m worth of damage, with one person sentenced for causing grievous bodily harm on a police officer who was hit with a sledgehammer.

schema.headline: US designates Palestine Action a terrorist group

title: Tim Curry: The Rocky Horror Picture Show star dies at 80
description: Born in Warrington in 1946, Curry's first acting job after university was in the original London production of groundbreaking rock musical Hair in 196
body: Born in Warrington in 1946, Curry's first acting job after university was in the original London production of groundbreaking rock musical Hair in 1968.In 1973, a fellow cast member, Richard O'Brien, asked Curry to audition for his new musical, and cast him in the role of the flamboyant lingerie-clad "sweet transvestite" Dr Frank-N-Furter.Curry first put his stamp on the character of the riotous scientist on stage in the upstairs theatre at London's Royal Court in 1973.The show's popularity snowballed and resulted in a big-screen adaptation, which also starred Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick and O'Brien.It was not an immediate hit at cinemas but became a fan favourite and holds the record for the longest-running theatrical release in film history.Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played the role in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be"."Being compared to you has been one of the greatest compliments I've ever received, even though it's a comparison no one could ever hope to live up to," he wrote in the letter.The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's deliver of the famous line from the musical, "Don't dream it, be it".A statement from Curry's representatives following his death said: "Across five decades, he moved fluidly between comedy, horror, drama, and music, delighting himself and his legion of fans with his countless dynamic personas."They added: "Few actors can claim to have left as many distinct fingerprints on pop culture - and though he suffered a debilitating stroke in 2012, he continued adding to his achievements as an artist and, most recently, a writer."Though widely known for his inimitable, flamboyant characters and colorful stage performances, his greatest legacies to those who knew him were his curious, expansive mind and generous, gentle heart, both of which remained open and filled with anticipation until his final breath."American comedy icon Carol Burnett, who shared a clip of Curry's turn as her smarmy brother in Annie alongside Bernadette Peters, wrote on social media that "nobody could play lovable villains better than he could".US actor Rob Schneider, who played the bell boy to Curry's uppity hotel clerk in Home Alone 2, said that he was "gutted" by Curry's death. "The sensational character actor, Tim Curry has left the stage," Schneider wrote. "A truly gifted performer of stage and screen, his one eyebrow could say more than most actors entire bodies. I am grateful to have the rare gift of watching him work, he made you better just standing near him."Curry had a major stroke in 2012 and had to use a wheelchair. He concentrated on voice acting and continued to appear at film conventions.His Clue co-star and Better Call Saul actor Michael McKean said on social that his last conversation with Curry was about "life and love and laughter"."The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend," he wrote.Curry published his memoir, titled Vagabond, last year.Grand Central Publishing said: "We are deeply saddened by the passing of Tim Curry, a singular talent whose extraordinary career left an indelible mark on generations of audiences."We are honored to have published his work and grateful for the stories, imagination, and joy he shared with readers."Our hearts are with his loved ones and countless fans around the world."His longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz confirmed he "passed away peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles on August 25".The Los Angeles Police Department told BBC News officers had responded to a death investigation for an 80-year-old man at 23:23 local time on Tuesday.Additional reporting by Tom Richardson and Nardine Saad.

schema.headline: Tim Curry: The Rocky Horror Picture Show star dies at 80

title: Portrait of Ann Widdecombe put up in Parliament for MPs' return
description: A portrait of Ann Widdecombe has been erected in Parliament to remember the former MP, who was found dead with serious head injuries last month.The pi
body: A portrait of Ann Widdecombe has been erected in Parliament to remember the former MP, who was found dead with serious head injuries last month.The picture of the ex-Conservative minister was put up on Tuesday in Portcullis House, where many MPs' offices are located, in time for the return from summer recess next week.It forms part of ongoing talks about a fitting memorial for the minister turned Reform UK spokeswoman, who died aged 78 after being found in her Devon home. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with murder.Helen Grant, Widdecombe's successor as MP for the area of Maidstone in Kent, said the portrait was "the start of a lasting tribute to Ann"."I am delighted that the Speaker of the House of Commons has confirmed that this portrait of Ann Widdecombe will be on show in Parliament, following her tragic death earlier this year," Grant said. Work is underway "to explore a more permanent commemoration on the Parliamentary estate", she added.The chosen photograph was taken in 2010 in the Cloister Corridor of the Palace of Westminster.

schema.headline: Portrait of Ann Widdecombe put up in Parliament for MPs' return

title: Rupert Grint to return to Harry Potter in Broadway play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rupert Grint said there was something "so special about stepping back into Ron's shoes now when we are both f
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rupert Grint said there was something "so special about stepping back into Ron's shoes now when we are both fathers"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterHarry Potter star Rupert Grint is to return to the role of Ron Weasley - playing the character as an adult in the spin-off play in New York.Grint was first cast to play Ron in the original films at the age of 11. Now 38, he will join the cast of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on Broadway for four months from next February.The play catches up with Harry, Ron and Hermione as grown-ups, 19 years after the end of the events in the original books and films - with Ron and Hermione now married and sending their daughter to Hogwarts."Dusting off the old robes. New York - see you all in February," Grint wrote on Instagram, external.Last November, he told BBC News he was unlikely to ever "step out" of Ron Weasley's shadow. "I'm fine with that. I think it's great," he said.Figure caption, November 2025: Would Rupert Grint step back into the Harry Potter universe?In a statement on Wednesday, the British actor said: "Ron Weasley has been a part of me since I was 11 years old and I can't wait to meet him again in this stage of life."There is something so full-circle and so special about stepping back into Ron's shoes now when we are both fathers; it is somehow both very familiar and completely new."And the joy of being back on Broadway, this time in a role that defined so much of my life is truly exciting."Grint is the only one of the main three stars from the films to return to their roles, although co-star Tom Felton is currently reprising his role as Draco Malfoy in the same play.They are not due to appear on stage together, however - Felton will appear until 3 January, with Grint joining on 2 February. He is currently scheduled to appear until 30 May.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Emma Watson, Daniel Radcliffe and Rupert Grint were introduced as Hermione, Harry and Ron in 2000Grint appeared in all eight Harry Potter films between 2001 and 2011, and has since starred in TV shows including Sick Note, Snatch and Servant.He also acted on Broadway in the comedy It's Only a Play in 2014.Harry Potter and the Cursed Child producers Sonia Friedman and Colin Callender said Grint's performances in the Potter films "defined for generations what it meant to be a loyal and brave friend even in the face of adversity and hardship".They added: "Rupert is not simply revisiting a role from his past. He is continuing a journey he began as a child and carrying it forward with all the life and experience he has gained since filming concluded, including a career that has taken him from film to television to acclaimed stage work on both Broadway and the West End."

schema.headline: Rupert Grint to return to Harry Potter in Broadway play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child

title: Pakistan PIMS fire: Witnesses say door was locked as Islamabad hospital blaze killed 14 babies
description: Figure caption, Watch: Hivsa Walid describes grabbing newborn and fleeing from hospital as fire ragedByCarrie Davies and Usman ZahidReporting fromPIMS
body: Figure caption, Watch: Hivsa Walid describes grabbing newborn and fleeing from hospital as fire ragedByCarrie Davies and Usman ZahidReporting fromPIMS hospital, IslamabadUpdated 7 hours agoIt was just after dawn on Wednesday morning at a maternity ward in the Pakistani capital when a horrific blaze erupted.It would go on to kill 14 infants as parents say they waited hours for help to arrive. Hivsa Walid was near the room at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital with her sister-in-law, who had given birth days earlier. She initially heard a shout and thought a patient had died - but then she saw smoke. The pair fled with the baby, who is so small she does not yet have a name."We didn't even think about our belongings. We just grabbed the baby and rushed downstairs."Some patients had delivered their babies just that night. I don't even know how we managed to get down - it was all a blur."The fire broke out in an air-conditioning unit on the third floor of the mother and child unit at PIMS, one of the main state-run hospitals in Islamabad. Only one of the 15 babies present was saved. Image source, ReutersImage caption, Eyewitnesses say proper evacuation protocols were not in place at the hospitalKhurram Mehmood, 40, told AFP news agency there was a long wait for rescue workers. "I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," he said.Jaweria, the mother of another victim, told AFP news agency the door to the maternity ward was locked."For two hours I kept crying and wailing," she said. "Police arrived after four hours and said they are here to investigate.""Why did the doctors leave the children there?" she asks. "To hell with you, rescue team and police. Babies burnt to death there, but nobody could save them."Rana Imran Sikander, the hospital's executive director, told the BBC the ward's door was not locked but was manned. He cited the need to protect babies from being stolen, something that has happened before at government hospitals.Figure caption, Scenes outside Pakistan hospital where newborn babies were killed in fireWalid suggested PIMS's safety protocols were inadequate, despite it being a major hospital. "There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything - everyone was just running."The father of a baby who died told Reuters he had been visiting the ward for eight days and the building had "no fire security, no proper exits". "All doors were closed, only one door was for us to visit our children. They kept the other doors locked because they feared we would come to see our children too often."Several eyewitnesses have claimed duty staff were not around.People had to "break the door down" and rescue teams were forced to smash the windows to control the flames, a witness who did not give her name told AFP.Abdul Ghafoor, another witness, told AFP he tried to get into the building to rescue patients but couldn't reach the maternity ward."There was thick black smoke inside and patients were trapped," he said. "Rescue teams arrived after almost two hours."Islamabad's Chief Commissioner Sohail Ashraf said rescue teams reached the scene "immediately" after the emergency call was first made, according to AFP.PIMS is one of the biggest hospitals in Pakistan's capital, with 156 beds in its maternal and child health unit.The country has dealt with a number of major fires in recent years, with poor safety laws, building codes and lax enforcement often blamed for steep death tolls.Survivors of a fire which killed dozens at a Karachi shopping mall in January this year said locked exits probably contributed to the high number of fatalities.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has expressed his "deep sorrow and heartfelt regret" over the latest blaze, and instructed authorities to "conduct an immediate investigation", according to a statement from his office.He has also suspended Federal Health Secretary Aslam Ghauri, a top official in the health department."Such a situation with children is irreparable," the statement said.

schema.headline: Pakistan PIMS fire: Witnesses say door was locked as Islamabad hospital blaze killed 14 babies

title: Football news: Uefa to push forward with plans to remove Gianni Infantino after dropping boycott threat
description: Uefa will press on with its attempt to remove Gianni Infantino as Fifa president despite withdrawing the threat to boycott competitions.The 55 member
body: Uefa will press on with its attempt to remove Gianni Infantino as Fifa president despite withdrawing the threat to boycott competitions.The 55 member associations, plus Europe's members on the Fifa Council, will on Thursday be presented with a letter which guarantees the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan will not be revived.The official removal of the boycott will be confirmed at Uefa's executive committee meeting in Monaco.That will satisfy Uefa's demands and mean the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup can go ahead next week in Poland with six European teams.But BBC Sport understands Uefa is confident that a unity candidate can be found to stand against Infantino when he is up for re-election in March.The vote is likely to be close, with the backing of 106 of the 211 member associations needed to be elected.However, Uefa has abandoned the idea of trying to force a vote of no confidence.It would require three quarters of the member associations, 159 votes, to pass the motion, which is considered unrealistic.No candidate has been identified, though Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is considered a serious option.Nominations must be submitted by 18 November.BBC Sport understands that any vote is expected to be close, and for that reason even if Infantino was to win it could cause terminal damage to his presidency, with his legitimacy compromised.Last month, European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the FFE proposal was dropped "in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership".After the boycott was dropped, Fifa welcomed the development, saying it is "pleased that all qualified teams will be participating in the upcoming Under-20 Women's World Cup".Six European teams - England, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain and hosts Poland - are scheduled to play in the tournament.A Fifa spokesperson said it "strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances" and Fifa "remains committed" to developing the game in "full dialogue with the confederations and stakeholders".On Tuesday, a group of former players published a statement saying "change is necessary" at the head of Fifa.Former Manchester United and France defender Mikael Silvestre, who sits on Fifa's Players' Voice Panel, issued a statement on X on Monday in a post he titled "Enough is Enough!".The statement has been shared on social media by the likes of England defender Lucy Bronze, France's 1998 World Cup winner Emmanuel Petit and former England goalkeeper David James.However on Wednesday, a different group of former players including World Cup-winning Brazil captain Cafu, former Italy striker Christian Vieri, former Portugal captain Pepe and ex-Argentina international Esteban Cambiasso all posted supportive messages for Infantino on social media.All of the players are so-called Fifa Legends, officially recognised by the governing body.Vieri's statement said: "Over the past 10 years, we have seen the work Fifa and President Infantino have done to create representativity for players in football, which did not exist."We will remain available to support the great evolution our game has seen this past decade, so that it keeps reaching and benefiting people of every country that plays football all around the world."

schema.headline: Football news: Uefa to push forward with plans to remove Gianni Infantino after dropping boycott threat

title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
description: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia IrelandUpdated 1 hour agoMassive landslides and flash floods on th
body: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia IrelandUpdated 1 hour agoMassive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.Search and rescue operations are under way. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss".Here is what we know so far.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Building were submerged in Nepal's Nuwakot districtWhat caused the deadly landslide?Nepal's foreign minister earlier said an earthquake was reported on the Tibet-Nepal border shortly before the landslide, suggesting it may have triggered the disaster.But the United States Geological Survey's latest analysis suggests there was no earthquake, raising questions about what caused the landslide itself.One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, but scientists say it is too soon to pinpoint its role in this specific event.Scientists are now trying to piece together the order of events.They'll be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.Figure caption, Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopterA deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.Severe flooding have been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Satellite images of Khadga Bhanjyang on the Trishuli River three days apart show the scale of floodingHow many people are dead and missing?The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. Nepal police have reported 157 bodies have been found, while China, which controls Tibet, says at least three people have died.However, the eventual death toll is expected to be much higher.According to Nepal's tourism board, 403 people are thought to be missing, including 341 foreign nationals, many from India.Other foreign nationals from 26 countries are also thought to have been caught up in the landslide, including 47 people from the US and 33 from the UK.Image source, ReutersHow are governments responding?Nepal's Prime Minister said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response. China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance". UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the British government will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.Figure caption, Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet borderWhat countries are the missing tourists from?Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including: India - the Nepal Tourism board said 142 nationals from neighbouring India were missingUkraine - Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said Nepal's Tourist Police informed them 53 Ukrainian nationals were missingMalaysia - seventeen Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels and are missing in the floods, the board saidUnited Kingdom - Nepal Police have confirmed that 33 British nationals are missingCanada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal said that 24 Canadians have been reported missingUS - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 54 US tourists are known to be among the missingSmaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, Australia and the Netherlands are also among the missing.

schema.headline: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods

title: Fires in Stourbridge which destroyed 19 homes started accidentally
description: Stourbridge fires that razed 19 homes accidentalImage source, ReutersImage caption, The day after the fires the government sent out an emergency alert
body: Stourbridge fires that razed 19 homes accidentalImage source, ReutersImage caption, The day after the fires the government sent out an emergency alertByElliot BallWest MidlandsUpdated 7 hours agoTwo fires that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge were started accidentally in fields where farming machinery was in use, according to West Midlands Fire Service.Investigators established agricultural equipment was being used in the vicinity of fields immediately before the fires were first reported. The service would not confirm the type of machinery.The first fire started in a field near Racecourse Lane at about 13:27 BST on 13 August, while a second began shortly afterwards in a field near Quarry Park Road.The day after the fires the government sent out an emergency alert to millions of people across England and Wales, warning them against "any activity that could start a fire".Image source, ReutersImage caption, The fires started in fields where agricultural machinery was being usedJustifying why the alert had been sent, Prime Minister Andy Burham said: "I was in Stourbridge today and saw first-hand the devastating impact these fires have had on people's homes and lives."The Stourbridge blaze was one of the most significant incidents West Midlands Fire Service had ever dealt with, Chief Fire Officer Simon Tuhill said. A major incident had been called as the wildfire spread across more than 500 acres and destroyed the 19 homes.Tuhill said on Wednesday so many people had been affected he wanted to confirm both fires were not started deliberately. They were accidental, he said."While investigations continue into the full circumstances of what happened, we wanted to share this latest update as soon as possible," he continued."I hope it will go some way towards helping people understand what happened on that exceptionally hot and challenging day."As well as the properties that were completely destroyed, a further 18 were damaged as the flames spread rapidly through grass and woodland.The incident in Stourbridge happened on the UK's hottest day of the year as temperatures peaked at 38.1C in some parts of the country, the Met Office said.Image caption, In Stourbridge, 19 homes were destroyed while 18 others were damaged in the fireSome residents were taken to Stourbridge Town Hall after the evacuation and given support by volunteers. The town also saw a great community effort as residents pulled together to help those in need and also to praise the farmers who had helped put the fires out.The Bishop of Dudley, the Right Reverend Martin Gorick, was among those who were forced to evacuate. "We saw houses going up in smoke in front of our eyes. Absolutely tragic," he said at the time.Robin and Loxie Williams saw their four-bedroom house destroyed. They had lived there for 26 years and said they had been forced to watch their neighbourhood going up in flames on TV.Image caption, Robin and Loxie Williams lost nearly everything in the fire"I know that many are still struggling to comprehend the scale of damage and personal loss," Tuhill added."I'm also acutely aware that this information will not bring those back homes, livelihoods or cherished memories.He added he was proud of the fire service response, plus that of colleagues in the police, ambulance and local farming community."The response to this incident showed the very best of Stourbridge and the wider West Midlands."Several other fires were reported in the West Midlands on the same day as a total of 54 patients were treated by paramedics and 19 were taken to hospital.Other incidents saw about a dozen homes lost in Birmingham, four in Stoke-on-Trent, three in Pershore, Worcestershire and three in Willenhall, near Wolverhampton.The causes of most are still under investigation, although it was confirmed a barbecue started the one in Stoke on Trent.

schema.headline: Fires in Stourbridge which destroyed 19 homes started accidentally

title: Why high energy bills look like they are here to stay
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentEnergy bills may have been a long way from our minds through the sweltering summer. Clothes on
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentEnergy bills may have been a long way from our minds through the sweltering summer. Clothes on a washing line have been drying in minutes. Cold showers have been more tempting than hot ones.But the latest news and forecasts on gas prices will bring a renewed sense of worry and urgency to families, as well as government ministers.Energy prices will rise by nearly 4% for millions of households in October. Even more striking is a prediction from the respected consultancy Cornwall Insight of a further 9% increase at the peak of winter in January.With ongoing volatility in the wholesale gas market sparked by events in the Gulf region, the energy sector says high prices are here to stay.EDF suggests bills will remain "stubbornly high" at their current level at least until the end of the decade.As prices rise, so does debtHigh bills have, and continue to, bite. Energy prices have been central to the cost-of-living squeeze.The typical household's dual-fuel bill is now 70% higher than it was at the start of 2021, before Russia's invasion of Ukraine. That amounts to around £600 more each year than pre-crisis levels, according to industry body Energy UK.Inevitably, more and more people have been unable to pay. Unpaid energy debt of more than three months is now at a record high, according to regulator Ofgem.Suppliers, who chart debt levels for missed payments of a month or more, estimate total unpaid bills and charges to have reached £6bn. By the end of the year, they expect that to rise to £7bn.The average household in debt, without a repayment plan, owes more than the typical annual bill.And even if you are not in debt, you pay. Covering the cost of debt already adds about £60 to the average annual bill. Consultancy Baringa says everyone could, on average, be paying £100 to cover the cost of unpaid debts by the end of the year.Someone who pays their bill on demand every three months, rather than a monthly direct debit, is typically already paying £150 a year to cover debt of others, owing to the greater risk of non-payment on this type of bill.So, pressure on the government to help those most in need will only intensify.Ofgem has a proposed debt relief scheme on the table, and campaigners keep telling them to get on with it, urging the government as to provide funding for it to be implemented.Image source, Getty ImagesCharities and the industry also want ministers to introduce a discounted tariff for those who need it most - based on benefits, health and income data.Energy UK says a targeted plan would cost £1.9bn. That would be much cheaper than the £40bn commitment to protect everyone's bills after Russia invaded Ukraine.But, who would pay? It could go on everyone else's bills. Or ministers could opt to raise taxes, borrow the money, or cancel spending elsewhere - all of which are tricky political choices.We've all done our bitThose who can have cut back on their energy use to reduce bills in recent years. Thermostats up and down the country have not been set as high as before. Batch cooking is more common.So much so that Ofgem's official calculations for typical energy consumption were lowered again in July (to 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year).Millions have shifted onto fixed tariffs, with 35% of billpayers on such a deal.So, many can justifiably say they have done their bit. Others who are older or who have health conditions might not have the luxury of lowering their energy use.So, community warm hubs have become popular. Some became cold hubs during the hot summer so people could make use of the air con.The heatwave has reduced the amount of energy stored across Europe, which needs to be restocked, piling more pressure on prices.Add to that the huge cost of upgrading the UK's electricity network and you can see why there are predictions of longstanding high energy bills - irrespective of whether a lasting peace in the Iran war brings down the international price of wholesale gas.All eyes on the BudgetIn the long-term, the government and Ofgem wants to shift the country away from our reliance on gas, with its volatile international pricing.Expect lots of fanfare over the sale, for the first time in the UK, of plug-in solar panels.In the short-term ministers - and the new prime minister - say they are helping where they can, and promising that there is "more to do".VAT will be cut on electricity bills in October. It means the price of electricity will fall, but that's been more than outstripped by an 8% rise in the price of gas.In the last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves cut some so-called policy costs and shifted some onto general taxation instead.Ministers may be tempted to do more of that, but could face be criticised for simply shifting the burden off bills and onto taxes.So, the options are limited. The new chancellor, John Healey, has choices to make - with lots of calls for help but with limited room for manoeuvre in the public finances.All eyes will be on his first Budget, which comes soon after those higher autumn energy bills kick in.Get in touchAre you affected by issues covered in this story?

schema.headline: Why high energy bills look like they are here to stay

title: We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy
description: He said Stacy was dealing with complex and conflicting circumstances - the fear that someone who "should" have been protecting her was dangerous, as w
body: He said Stacy was dealing with complex and conflicting circumstances - the fear that someone who "should" have been protecting her was dangerous, as well as "fear from outsiders looking in"."If somebody is controlling, when that creeps in, it's probably going to be very difficult to get out of that situation," said Sean."I think that's what we witnessed over a long period of time, but… it's hard to know what you can do. Because you don't want to get fully into other people's business – their family, household and everything else."Ann said Stacy also had to consider stability for her children."She wanted to keep them in their own home, in their own routine, with their own school, neighbours, friends, the animals around them," she said."She felt 'why should she run?' Although she was scared she still felt kind of protected with the kids."Stacy's case has made a significant impact on her community – a campaign calling for a "Stacy's law" has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed.Lynne's petition, which Stacy's family supports, calls for high-risk domestic abuse perpetrators or suspects released on bail to have their location monitored using GPS equipment.This could include individually assessed exclusion zones around victim's homes or workplaces and alerts that trigger police responses when conditions are breached.Scottish ministers have previously faced criticism over the slow rollout of Global Positioning System (GPS) equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries.Mike Nellis, emeritus professor of criminal and community justice at the University of Strathclyde and one of the UK's leading experts on electronic monitoring, said it was perfectly feasible to introduce such a system.But he cautioned that no system was fool proof, and that some women's support groups have in the past voiced concern that such systems might give a false sense of security.He said: "I think probably every jurisdiction that has used it has at one point in time had an offender who still managed to assault, injure or kill the victim."The Scottish government said it was listening to victims and support organisations and would carefully consider the petition.Sean and Ann now consider Stacy's death to be confirmation that "signs [of abuse] are real and need to be addressed".Mair was ordered by a court not to approach Stacy, but Ann said that any warnings he received would have made no impact given everything she had seen of his character."There was nothing in place to deter him or make him think about it, of consequences, no fear," she said."It was only a piece of paper in the end to him and someone telling him not to do it. With his coercive and controlling behaviour, he wouldn't listen to it."Ann and Sean are due to meet First Minister John Swinney on Thursday to discuss what can be done to better support women facing similar circumstances.Scotland's victims minister, Kirsten Oswald, said her thoughts were with Stacy's family.She said: "As the first minister has made clear, government has a vital role to play in tackling violence against women and girls, but lasting change requires all of us to play our part."Men, in particular, must challenge sexism, confront abusive behaviour and help create a culture where every woman and girl can live free from violence, abuse and fear."While decisions on bail and remand are always a matter for the independent court, bail can be electronically monitored."Stacy's family now prefer her to be remembered by her pre-marriage surname Hunter, rather than her husband's name Mair.Radio Scotland Mornings examined Lynne McKenzie's petition in a series on violence against women - you can listen to the full programme here.If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy

title: Canal killer John Sweeney, who dismembered victims, dies in jail
description: A double killer who murdered and dismembered two women before dumping their bodies in canals in London and the Netherlands has died in prison.John Swe
body: A double killer who murdered and dismembered two women before dumping their bodies in canals in London and the Netherlands has died in prison.John Sweeney, 69, was serving a whole-life sentence after being convicted in 2011 of the murders of his former girlfriends.Paula Fields, 31, was killed in London. Parts of her body were found in six holdalls floating in Regent's Canal in Camden in February 2001. Her head, hands and feet were never recovered.Melissa Halstead, 33, from the US, was killed in 1990. Her dismembered body was found in a canal in Rotterdam, but she was not identified for 18 years.Sweeney is understood to have died at HMP Whitemoor in Cambridgeshire on 14 August.Police found hundreds of violent paintings and poems at Sweeney's north London home, including artwork depicting a bloodied axe and references to himself as the "Scalp Hunter".Police suspected he had murdered other former partners who had not been seen for years.He had previously been jailed for attempting to murder former girlfriend Delia Balmer in a 1994 axe attack in north London. Balmer later wrote a memoir about her experiences, which was adapted into the ITV drama Until I Kill You in 2024.A prison service spokesperson described the crimes as "horrific" and said their thoughts remained with the victims and their loved ones.As with all deaths in custody, the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman is investigating.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Burnham calls summit of first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
description: Burnham said: "I am in South Wales today because the answers to the UK's challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places
body: Burnham said: "I am in South Wales today because the answers to the UK's challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act."Good jobs in every community, in every part of the UK. That is what I want every leader in this country signed up to."He will meet the Welsh government's deputy first minister Sioned Williams at the visit.Williams said the visit was "a positive example of governments working together to improve people's lives".She will call for a "fair share of the UK government's steel fund", an "energy social tariff to support those facing fuel poverty and struggling with high energy bills", and high standing charges in Wales to be addressed.She added: "Wales is an energy-rich nation. People should see that reflected in good jobs, stronger communities and lower bills."The National Economic Council was created by the Gordon Brown administration in 2008, and has been revived by Burnham. A previous meeting brought together government ministers and English local authority mayors.Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to discuss "how we will drive good growth in every postcode across the UK" with the first ministers.The Welsh government said: "We look forward to discussing shared challenges, including ensuring growth and investment in all the countries represented, and support for families facing the continuing cost-of-living crisis."This is alongside further discussions with the UK government to progress broader priorities in Wales, including fair funding and extending devolution."Plaid Cymru has pressed the UK government for discussions over more powers and funding for the Senedd - Wales's parliament - and the Welsh government in Cardiff.First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth had his first meeting with the new prime minister on the sidelines of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in July.At the time, ap Iorwerth said it was "too early" to know whether the new Labour prime minister would agree to his calls.Downing Street said then that the prime minister wanted an "open and ongoing dialogue" with the first minister.

schema.headline: Burnham calls summit of first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland

title: Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children
description: Social media giant Meta has agreed to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed
body: Social media giant Meta has agreed to a $18bn (£13.3bn) settlement with US states and territories to resolve claims that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. A California judge approved the settlement, which Meta must pay to 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories, marking the company's largest payment over child safety litigation to date.Meta will also implement a host of changes aimed at better protecting kids online, which the states had demanded, including default daily time limits and night-time blocks."This is a major moment to clean up an industry that has been hurting our kids", California Attorney General Rob Bonta said.Meta has denied any wrongdoing as part of the settlement and said on Wednesday that the payment it agreed to "will be distributed in annual instalments over a 10-year period".Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers approved the settlement, writing that it "reflects a fair, reasonable, comprehensive, and good faith approach not only to provide monetary relief, but importantly, to change conduct in a way that attempts to meaningfully address the negative impacts of the social media platforms at issue". While the settlement includes almost the entire US, the initial lawsuit was filed in 2023 by 29 states accusing the company of numerous violations of federal and state child privacy laws.One of the states that was not part of the settlement was New Mexico. Last month, a federal judge there handed down a historic ruling against Meta, finding it to be a "public nuisance" on par with air pollution and ordering it to pay combined fines of almost $1bn.    As a jury trial kicked off last week in an Oakland, California, federal court, state lawyers argued the tech company knew that millions of 11- and 12-year-old users were on Instagram and Facebook over the years, yet "did little to keep them off" the platforms.Although the trial had only gone on for five days, state lawyers relied heavily on information found in millions of internal Meta documents provided in the case. They included internal research, employee emails, and chat logs that went all the way up to chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.One piece of internal research on Instagram stated: "Teens have an addict's narrative about use." Still, the states argued, Meta targeted young users."The trial did not go well for Meta," Bonta said on Wednesday. Meta maintained throughout the brief trial that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for its youngest users, pouring resources into testing and research, and building new features."We're always working on teen safety," head of Instagram Adam Mosseri said during an hour of court testimony on Tuesday. The case was settled and court adjourned before he could reappear before a jury.Before Mosseri's testimony, a former researcher at Meta, George Volichenko, appeared and with lawyers went over various internal communications he had been a part of regarding Meta's work on safety.Volichenko said he struggled to understand when he was at the company in 2022 why the team he worked on wasn't given more freedom to better test and implement new safety features. One of those was "quiet mode", which muted notifications for teen users during the night. His team knew such a feature would be much more widely adopted if Meta turned it on by default.He recalled his manager telling him he "shouldn't worry too much about the adoption figures being low, because the team exists partially to protect the company against the upcoming lawsuits".As part of the Wednesday settlement, however, a feature called "night mode", which blocks notifications between midnight and 6am, will now be on by default - meaning they will be turned on automatically. The settings are also designed only to be turned off by a parent or guardian."The framework we've negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms," CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said.Other features for teen users being implemented as part of the deal include:A default two-hour daily time limit (cumulative across Instagram and Facebook) that teens can only turn off with a parent's permission.Likes will be hidden, on teens' profiles and those that they interact with."School mode", or a mute on notifications between 08:00 and 15:00 during school days.Prompts noting when a teen has hit 15 minutes of continual use. Then notifications when cumulative use has hit 60 and 90 minutes.The ability to choose a feed that is not driven by an algorithm.The ability to turn off autoplay for videos and content.Extreme make-up filters will no longer be accessible.As for the new daily time limit for teen users, that will be reduced to one hour of total daily use should other social media platforms like TikTok, Snap and YouTube also agree to implement new restrictions for young users.Bonta urged such platforms to do so, saying the settlement with Meta "is a good blueprint" for other companies to follow. Should they not, he suggested on Wednesday that his office would now be "more focused" on bringing changes to the entire social media industry.Meta also said TikTok and YouTube should implement the same safety features for their younger users."Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta's Mahoney said.YouTube and TikTok have been contacted for comment. District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb called the Meta deal a "monumental public health victory".He added: "The safety features Meta is required to install will fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook."

schema.headline: Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children

title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move
description: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believ
body: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California, and landed in Birmingham shortly before midday.A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on". There did not appear to be a police presence as Harry and his family left the airport, a source told the BBC.Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.Though not confirming the family's arrival in the UK, a spokesman for the Sussexes did say their chickens were staying in California, but they were bringing their dogs Mia and Pula with them.The chickens, which the couple rescued, have regularly featured on Meghan's Instagram account and also appeared in her Netflix programme.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move
